video_title: Recursive's $670M Bet on Self-Improving AI, Sonnet 5.5 Hits 70%, Elon Co-Leads Pentagon Push EP 299
gist: Richard, founder of you.com and CEO of Recursive (fresh off a $670M raise), argues weak recursive self-improvement already exists and strong RSI takes off next year, yet sees full ASI as decades away, a timeline the hosts reject. The panel also covers his Eureka Machine AI-for-science thesis, Ro Khanna's proposed RSI ban and p(doom), Gemini 4 Argon and Sonnet 5.5 cost-performance critiques, a GPU compute crunch, and the Pentagon's Musk/Luckey-led Project Meridian.

themes.theme: Recursive's RSI thesis and ASI timelines

insights.claim: Richard says AI's new ability to code closes a loop (AI is code and AI can code), so weak forms of recursive self-improvement already exist, with strong RSI expected to take off next year.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: RSI is a near-term (2027) capability inflection, not a distant one.
insights.quote: We already have RSI. We're not quite there yet, but we're very close.

insights.claim: Richard argues the labs' current practice of engineers using Codex or Claude to write lab code is only weak RSI because humans remain deeply embedded; Recursive aims to have humans set only rewards, environments and goals while AI owns ideation, implementation and validation.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Defines what differentiates Recursive from frontier labs' internal AI-assisted R&D.
insights.quote: you still have like deeply embedded humans in that loop

insights.claim: Strong RSI requires inner loops for ideation, implementation and validation all run by AI, plus an outer open-ended evolutionary process that recombines interestingly different ideas, akin to biological, cultural and technological evolution.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Open-endedness/evolutionary search is the core research bet at Recursive.

insights.claim: The binding physical constraint on RSI is compute: an RSI system needs large compute budgets to train sophisticated versions of itself.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: RSI progress scales with capital for compute, explaining the large raise and compute deals.
insights.quote: you still need a lot of compute

insights.claim: Recursive raised $670 million from Google Ventures, Greycroft, Nvidia and AMD plus $410 million in compute from AWS; Richard indicated a roughly $450 million compute spend may have been one of its smallest compute deals.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Signals Recursive is a well-capitalized new frontier-scale RSI lab backed by chip vendors.
insights.quote: that may have been one of the smallest comput deals we've done

insights.claim: No one has yet automated the choice of which self-improvement axes to optimize (parameters, training data, objective, architecture, code/harness), evidenced by big labs still hiring thousands of engineers.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Lab hiring of engineers is a tell for how far true RSI is.
insights.quote: all the big companies are still hiring thousands of engineers

insights.claim: Richard defines ASI as surpassing all of humanity combined across ten spaces of intelligence (perceptual, communication, social, creative, speed, metacognition, knowledge, reasoning, etc.) with some ability to choose what it works on, and expects that to take several decades.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Contrarian long ASI timeline from an RSI founder; spiky superhuman capabilities come much sooner.
insights.quote: to be better than all of humanity combined I think will take us probably several decades

insights.claim: Richard expects AI to be better than all of humanity at programming and math within a few years, but physical-world constraints such as building new ASML-class lithography machines and supply chains will slow full ASI.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect spiky domain superintelligence (code, math, games) well before general physical-world dominance.
insights.quote: it will take more than 2 years to build such a machine even if you had the perfect blueprint

insights.claim: Alex rejects the multi-decade ASI timeline, arguing hooking AI to the physical world is the easy part and that Elon's free-electron laser could replace ASML within about three years; Peter agrees with Alex.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Hosts see a much faster ASI path than the guest; timeline dispersion is wide even among insiders.
insights.quote: Completely don't buy the 20-year timeline.

insights.claim: Richard believes a perfected post-RSI model will not cleanly separate world knowledge from a small reasoning kernel; some world knowledge must live in weights for creative reasoning, with external search as a complement.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Argues against the 'megabyte reasoning core + database' end state; retrieval remains complementary.
insights.quote: It's not going to be a perfect separation for sure.

insights.claim: Alex notes the nanoGPT speedrun record collapsed from roughly 60-70 seconds to about 40 seconds via algorithmic changes, including factoring out world knowledge, sparking controversy; Richard teased another update within days.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Algorithmic RSI-style gains without more data are compounding fast; watch for Recursive's announcement.

insights.claim: Richard's book The Eureka Machine argues AI will deliver a century of scientific breakthroughs in a decade by automating the full scientific stack using LLM world knowledge, digitized scientific data, simulations, robotic lab automation and agent swarms.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames full-stack AI science as the main value driver of AI.

insights.claim: Richard argues scientific progress slowed due to fragmentation into ever-narrower subdisciplines rather than underfunding, and AI can weave the pieces back together.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Interdisciplinary AI systems target a structural, not funding, bottleneck in R&D.

insights.claim: Richard predicts multiple simpler, single-gene diseases will be cured in the next 12 months, with progress thereafter set by how much money is put into compute rather than a single threshold.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Near-term gene-therapy wins; science output becomes a function of compute spend.
insights.quote: multiple different diseases will get cured in the next 12 months

insights.claim: New-generation biotechs run 5 to 10 compounds in phase three trials within 2-3 years, versus the old model of one drug over 10 years, but FDA-gated human approvals still impose half-a-decade-to-a-decade delays.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Biotech pipelines are diversifying faster; regulatory timelines remain the bottleneck for disease cures.
insights.quote: they have 5 to 10 different compounds in uh stage three trials after 2 or 3 years

insights.claim: Richard believes biology, not physics, is the biggest domain for AI because neural nets excel at modeling complex interactions among well-understood parts, while physics data collection requires billion-dollar facilities like the Large Hadron Collider.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Pushes AI-for-science capital toward biology over fundamental physics.
insights.quote: I think the biggest domain is actually going to be biology.

insights.claim: Richard applies the bitter lesson to biology: experts doubt one model can absorb their domain, but massive perturbation datasets from companies like Tahoe Therapeutics will make simple, scaled models win.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Data-generation companies for biology are a key investable layer.

insights.claim: Richard's rule is that AI becomes superhuman in any domain that can be simulated or verified; virtual cell models are the third pillar, though cells can't yet be fully measured without destroying them.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Investment test: back AI applications in domains with simulators or cheap verifiers.
insights.quote: anything you can simulate, anything you can verify, AI will then be able to solve things in that domain

insights.claim: Parallel Bio grows lymph-node organoids from pluripotent stem cells and obtained FDA approval to skip animal trials because its parallel organoid tests better predict human drug response and toxicity.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Organoid platforms can compress preclinical timelines and displace animal testing.
insights.quote: they got FDA approval to skip animal trials

insights.claim: Lila Sciences is building a scientific superintelligence running about a million square feet of robotic lab space to raise discovery rates roughly a thousandfold; Periodic Labs pursues a similar approach in physics and chemistry.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Autonomous wet labs are a core infrastructure bet in AI-for-science.

insights.claim: Dave relays that MIT mathematicians are pivoting to AI orchestration while biology professors are in denial and use almost no AI; Richard says economics is even further behind in adopting AI for policy.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Academic biology and economics are laggard fields ripe for AI disruption.

themes.theme: Doomerism, regulation and the RSI ban

insights.claim: Rep. Ro Khanna is introducing the Human Control Over AI Act, which would ban recursively self-improving models until federal guardrails exist, with criminal penalties and government-reporting auditors embedded in every frontier lab; a cited poll shows 68% voter support.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Direct legislative risk to RSI labs including Recursive.

insights.claim: Richard argues enforcing an RSI ban would require an unprecedented totalitarian surveillance state, since anyone with a laptop GPU can prompt an AI to improve its own harness in about 20 minutes.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: RSI bans are practically unenforceable without thought-police-level surveillance.
insights.quote: This is something you can literally hack up in like 20 minutes with prompt engineering

insights.claim: Richard states p(doom) is zero, arguing that once sci-fi scenarios are removed, realistic worst cases (bioweapons, cyber, AI-driven cults) are bounded harms best addressed by regulating applications, as with the internet.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Advocates application-level regulation over model-level restrictions.
insights.quote: P doom is zero

insights.claim: Richard criticizes doomer scenarios for granting attackers near-magical abilities while never giving defenders equivalent abilities.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Offense-defense symmetry argument against catastrophic-risk framing.
insights.quote: somehow the defenders in those stories never get near magical abilities to defend

insights.claim: Dave and Alex argue the real threat to AI progress is not arrests but corporate liability and class actions, which could make Anthropic stop offering its best models broadly and keep them in-house.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Liability regimes are a larger tail risk to open model access than bans.
insights.quote: that's what'll actually grind it to a halt long before arrests and convictions

insights.claim: Peter warns a possible Democratic House plus 70-80% of Americans opposing data centers and fearing ASI could produce restrictive policy despite being illogical.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Political risk to AI infrastructure buildout is rising with public opinion.

insights.claim: Dave says Elon was right to call out Dario for declaring Mythos potentially dangerous and then releasing it 30 days later, a communication misstep that fed public fear.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Lab safety messaging can backfire into political backlash.

insights.claim: Richard calls Anthropic's constitution 'fake' because it lists never creating cyber weapons as a hard constraint, yet Glasswing and Anthropic's models were used to hack systems.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Questions the credibility of constitutional AI safety claims.
insights.quote: it was a cool marketing gimmick but it just didn't work

insights.claim: Richard argues reward hacking is the real alignment problem and capitalism will solve it because no customer pays for AI that doesn't solve the actual problem; liability-bearing firms like Hippocratic AI already staff large teams to ensure correctness.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Reward engineering becomes a job category; liability drives reliability.
insights.quote: reward engineering will become a real job

themes.theme: Frontier model race: Gemini 4 Argon, Sonnet 5.5, compute crunch

insights.claim: In one week Google shipped Gemini 4 Argon, Anthropic shipped Sonnet 5.5 and OpenAI shipped GPT 6.1, while frontier intelligence got about threefold cheaper.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Release cadence and price deflation continue rapidly.
insights.quote: Frontier Intelligence has gotten cheaper by three-fold

insights.claim: Gemini 4 Argon raised output limits from 64,000 to 1 million tokens and follows a never-shipped Gemini 3.5 Pro, but Alex says it ranks third on Artificial Analysis behind Anthropic and OpenAI and is off the cost-performance frontier, with cherry-picked benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Google remains a #3 frontier lab despite resources.
insights.quote: it puts them back in the top three frontier labs after Anthropic and OpenAI. It does not put them in the top two.

insights.claim: Alex says Google is compute-starved because of an internal 'knife fight' for GPUs/TPUs between Google Cloud, Search/Ads and DeepMind.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Internal compute allocation, not capital, may cap Google's frontier position.
insights.quote: it's still an internal knife fight

insights.claim: Alex theorizes Argon's standout low hallucination reflects its dual mandate to serve Google Search answers, and that near-zero hallucination effectively turns the model into a monetizable search index, consistent with Google's renewed sale of search API access.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Google's model strategy may be optimized for search, not superintelligence.

insights.claim: Sonnet 5.5 jumped from 10% to 70% on Terminal Bench 4.0, beating Opus 5.5's 66.4% at half the price, and is the first Sonnet launched with cyber safeguards.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Large single-generation jump in agentic command-line capability.
insights.quote: Sonnet 5.5 jumped from 10% to 70%

insights.claim: Alex says Sonnet 5.5 is below Opus 5.5 on a cost-per-attempt performance basis, unlike typical distilled smaller models, so he sees no reason to use it absent token or latency constraints.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Pricing anomaly undercuts Sonnet 5.5's value proposition.
insights.quote: I do not plan to use Sonnet 5.5

insights.claim: Dave theorizes Anthropic priced Sonnet 5.5 to keep enterprises full-stack Anthropic rather than orchestrating Opus with cheap Chinese open models like Kimi K3 or Qwen, with China about three months behind.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Open-weight Chinese models pressure frontier lab pricing in enterprise orchestration.
insights.quote: China, which is about three months behind

insights.claim: Richard says there is a compute crunch: prices for GB200 clusters and even seven-year-old H100s have risen recently; Dave lost an NVL72 order at $3M to a $5M bidder. Richard expects more supply in about two years with fluctuating, not crashing, prices.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: GPU scarcity and pricing power persist; old GPUs aren't depreciating to zero.
insights.quote: the price of H100s has uh gone up uh in in a crazy way

themes.theme: New AI products: decision models, video Turing test, BCI

insights.claim: Tavus unveiled Griffin, a full-duplex interactive video model that 48% of people mistook for a human in live video chats versus 3% for prior systems; it tops Nvidia's full-duplex benchmark but is withheld pending safety work.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Real-time human-passing avatars threaten service-sector jobs and enable scams.
insights.quote: 48% of people who talk to an AI avatar on a live face-to-face video thought they were talking to a real human

insights.claim: Alex says Chinese labs such as Alibaba remain overinvested relative to Western labs in interactive generative video, and predicts end-to-end generated real-time video will automate many face-and-voice service jobs.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Interactive video is a US-China competition front and service-sector disruption vector.

insights.claim: Typesafe AI's Jev is a 'system one' decision model that outputs categorical, numeric or binary answers in milliseconds; OpenAI has already launched a decisions API and open-source clones exist, so Alex views the concept as easily commoditized.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Fast classifiers are returning but offer little moat.

insights.claim: Salim argues most organizational decisions are micro system-one choices, so routing them to near-free decision models collapses the cost of micro-coordination; Jev is named for the Jevons paradox.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail
insights.so_what: Enables massive automation of enterprise micro-decisions.
insights.quote: the cost of microcoordination collapses

insights.claim: Alex says Neuralink announced its first scaling-law studies for pre-training foundation models on Neuralink electrode data, noting fMRI is limited to about cubic-millimeter and ~1-second resolution, insufficient for full-bandwidth BCI.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Invasive high-resolution BCI data is the path to brain foundation models.

themes.theme: Defense, biology policy and the post-AI economy

insights.claim: Defense Secretary Hegseth announced Project Meridian, co-led by Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey with Newt Gingrich and overseen by Pentagon CTO Emil Michael, with findings due in 120 days; SpaceX and Anduril hold multi-billion-dollar defense contracts.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Tech-founder influence over defense procurement is rising, benefiting SpaceX and Anduril.

insights.claim: Alex highlights the stand-up of the Department of War's first Autonomous Warfare Command, a four-star functional combatant command, and flags seabed and cislunar domains as underserved areas likely to see investment.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Autonomous systems, seabed and cislunar tech gain dedicated defense demand.
insights.quote: This I think is a transformative moment

insights.claim: Salim says Russia and Ukraine will each make about 10 million drones this year, up from roughly half a million used two years into the war, and about 10,000 drones a month cross the US-Mexico border.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail
insights.so_what: Drone production is scaling exponentially; linear procurement can't keep up.
insights.quote: you can't find exponential technology with linear procurement

insights.claim: A presidential executive order directs agencies to cut invasive mosquitoes in Washington DC by 90% and ticks by 50% by 2028, prioritizing sterile insects, genetic modification and beneficial bacteria over pesticides; Alex calls it the first federal mandate enabling gene drives.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Federal tailwind for gene-drive and synthetic-biology vector control.

insights.claim: Richard argues AI job impact depends on demand elasticity: illustration demand didn't expand when prices fell from $200 to cents, so illustrators lost jobs, whereas personalized software will see Jevons-style demand growth.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Use price elasticity to predict which industries AI shrinks versus grows.

insights.claim: Richard says bots and agents already outnumber humans online, and in an abundant society attention, fame and brand become scarcer currencies, so the attention economy grows even as agent purchasing pressures platforms like Amazon.
insights.speaker: Richard (Recursive CEO)
insights.so_what: Brand and attention assets appreciate; agent commerce disintermediates platforms.

insights.claim: Dave says a single big data center like Abilene, Texas is worth about half a trillion dollars versus about $4 trillion for all cars, implying insurable assets will rise sharply; Salim says liability shifts from drivers to layers of the autonomous stack.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Insurance shifts toward data centers, robots and software liability.
